single-degenerate-model.title: Single-Degenerate Model
single-degenerate-model.content:
Accreting mass steadily from a close, non-degenerate binary companion onto a carbon-oxygen white dwarf drives the stellar remnant toward a critical density. This evolutionary pathway, which represents a prominent channel for Type Ia supernovae progenitors, requires a fine-tuned balance between the mass transfer rate and the thermal timescale of the receiving star. To achieve stable hydrogen shell burning on the surface of the white dwarf without triggering periodic classical nova explosions, the accretion rate must fall within a narrow parameter space, typically between \(10^{-8}\) and \(10^{-7}\) solar masses per year, written as \(\dot{M} \in [10^{-8}, 10^{-7}] M_{\odot}/\text{yr}\). If the accretion rate is too low, the hydrogen layer becomes degenerate and ignites explosively as a nova, ejecting the accumulated mass. If the rate is too high, the star expands into a red giant configuration, leading to common envelope evolution.

The critical accretion rate for stable burning depends on the mass of the white dwarf \(M_{\text{WD}}\), which increases as matter is deposited onto the core. The mathematical relation defining this stable accretion window is given by \(\dot{M}_{\text{crit}} \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-7} (M_{\text{WD}}/M_{\odot} - 0.7) M_{\odot}/\text{yr}\). As the white dwarf approaches the Chandrasekhar mass limit, which is approximately \(M_{\text{Ch}} \approx 1.4 M_{\odot}\), the electrons in the core become highly relativistic. The pressure supporting the star is no longer a simple function of density, but is governed by the relativistic energy-momentum relation \(E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2\) where \(p\) is the electron momentum and \(m_0\) is the electron rest mass. This relativistic equation of state indicates that the pressure scales as \(P \propto \rho^{4/3}\) instead of the non-relativistic \(P \propto \rho^{5/3}\), making the star unstable to gravitational collapse.

During this accretion phase, the potential energy released by the falling gas is converted into heat and radiation, producing a high-energy luminosity \(L = G M_{\text{WD}} \dot{M} / R_{\text{WD}}\), where \(R_{\text{WD}}\) is the radius of the white dwarf. The thermal structure of the envelope is modeled by integrating the stellar structure equations on a spherical manifold, ensuring that the energy flux satisfies the radiative transport equations with coordinate index \(\mu\) and radius \(r\), where the energy flux \(F(r)\) is computed. At the microphysical scale, the incoming hydrogen undergoes thermonuclear fusion to produce helium, which forms a shell beneath the hydrogen layer. This helium layer eventually ignites in a similar manner, growing the carbon-oxygen core toward the critical ignition density. The conservation of energy and momentum during these shell-burning phases is critical for ensuring that the white dwarf steadily grows in mass rather than losing its envelope to stellar winds.

On galactic scales, these accreting binary systems are nested within dark matter halos that shape the gravitational potential fields of host galaxies. The spatial distribution of these supernovae progenitors can be modeled using the inflaton field parameters that dictated the primordial density fluctuations in the early universe, which eventually collapsed to form the first stars and galaxies. By studying the environmental dependencies of Type Ia supernovae, such as the age and metallicity of the host galaxy, astronomers can constrain the delay-time distribution of these events, which represents the time elapsed between the formation of the binary system and its subsequent explosion at redshift \(z\) with delay-time parameter \(t_d\) and mass ratio \(f = M_2/M_1\). This delay-time distribution helps distinguish between the single-degenerate model and the double-degenerate model, where the supernova is triggered by the merger of two white dwarfs.

Thermonuclear runaway begins at the center of the white dwarf when the density reaches approximately \(\rho_c \approx 2 \times 10^9 \text{ g/cm}^3\), igniting carbon fusion under highly degenerate conditions. Because the degenerate electron pressure is independent of temperature, the increase in temperature due to fusion does not cause the star to expand and cool, leading to a runaway thermonuclear explosion. The propagation of the fusion flame through the core is modeled using a nuclear equation of state, which couples the nuclear reaction rates to the hydrodynamic expansion of the plasma. The resulting explosion completely disrupts the star, leaving no compact remnant and synthesizing a large amount of radioactive nickel-56 \(^{56}\text{Ni}\), which decays to cobalt-56 \(^{56}\text{Co}\) and eventually stable iron-56 \(^{56}\text{Fe}\), powering the observed light curve of the supernova.

Taking the limit where the companion mass and the accretion rate approach zero allows physicists to recover the static cooling equations of a single degenerate star. In this non-accreting limit where \(\dot{M} \to 0\), the time-dependent term in the stellar structure equations vanishes, and the system simplifies to the classical Lane-Emden equation for a polytrope of index \(n = 3\) or \(n = 1.5\). The complex shell-burning physics decouples from the core dynamics, and the white dwarf simply radiates its stored thermal energy into the vacuum. This smooth mathematical reduction verifies that the accretion model is consistent with the standard theory of static white dwarfs, satisfying the correspondence principle across all scales and ensuring that the description of physical reality remains ontologically secure.

bra-ket-notation.title: Bra-Ket Notation (Dirac Notation)
bra-ket-notation.content:
Representing quantum states as abstract vectors in Hilbert space forms the mathematical cornerstone of modern quantum mechanics. The primary language used to express these vectors is bra-ket notation, developed by Paul Dirac to simplify the algebraic manipulation of state vectors and operators. In this notation, a physical state is represented by a contravariant vector called a ket, written as \(|\psi\rangle\), which contains all the observable information about the physical system. The superposition principle asserts that any linear combination of kets, such as \(c_1 |\psi_1\rangle + c_2 |\psi_2\rangle\), is also a valid state vector in the Hilbert space at coordinate positions \(x^\mu\). This linear structure allows quantum fields to exist in combinations of multiple states simultaneously, mapping physical realities onto a continuous manifold. The mathematical structure of this vector space guarantees that all physical predictions remain consistent under any choice of basis, ensuring coordinate independence for all quantum mechanical formulations.

For every ket \(|\psi\rangle\) in the vector space, there exists a corresponding covariant vector in the dual space called a bra, represented by the symbol \(\langle\psi|\). The bra space is a vector space of linear functionals that map kets onto complex numbers, serving as the mathematical representation of measurement devices or reference frames. A bra is constructed from its corresponding ket by taking the Hermitian conjugate, meaning that \(\langle\psi| = (|\psi\rangle)^\dagger\). This bra-ket duality is a direct manifestation of the Riesz representation theorem, which establishes an isomorphism between the vector space and its dual, ensuring that the geometric structure of the Hilbert space is preserved under complex conjugation. This mapping allows us to define the projection of a state vector onto any coordinate axis, facilitating the calculation of spatial wave functions.

When a bra and a ket are combined, they form a bracket, written as \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\), which represents the inner product of the two vectors. This complex number quantifies the overlap between the two states, and according to the Born rule, its squared magnitude determines the transition probability \(P = |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2\) of finding the system in state \(|\phi\rangle\) after being prepared in state \(|\psi\rangle\). The inner product satisfies the requirement of positive-definiteness, ensuring that the norm of a state, \(\|\psi\| = \sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}\), is a real, non-negative number that is equal to one for a normalized state. This normalization is essential for ensuring that the sum of all probabilities equals exactly one, maintaining the causal structure of physical interactions and preventing the occurrence of unphysical singular states with infinite probability.

The notation also facilitates the description of linear operators, which act on kets to transform them into new vectors within the Hilbert space. An operator \(\hat{A}\) acting on a ket \(|\psi\rangle\) is written as \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle\), and its expectation value in that state is given by the bracket \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle\). The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of these operators correspond to the measurable values and the resulting states of physical observables, such as energy or momentum. The Hermitian conjugate of the operator, denoted as \(\hat{A}^\dagger\), satisfies the relation \(\langle\phi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = \langle\hat{A}^\dagger\phi|\psi\rangle\), and physical observables are represented by self-adjoint operators where \(\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger\), ensuring that their eigenvalues are always real numbers and that measurement outcomes are physically meaningful.

Outer products are constructed by placing a ket next to a bra, written as \(|\phi\rangle\langle\psi|\), which represents a linear operator that maps any vector onto the direction of \(|\phi\rangle\). A critical application of this outer product is the resolution of the identity, which states that the sum of the outer products of a complete orthonormal basis \(\{|i\rangle\}\) is equal to the identity operator, written as \(\sum |i\rangle\langle i| = \hat{I}\). This resolution allows any arbitrary state vector \(|\psi\rangle\) to be expanded in terms of the basis states as \(|\psi\rangle = \sum c_i |i\rangle\), where the coefficients are given by the brackets \(c_i = \langle i|\psi\rangle\), simplifying the calculation of matrix elements and coordinate representations. This completeness relation is crucial for constructing the propagator in path integral formulations.

Taking the classical limit of these quantum mechanical representations is achieved by examining the behavior of the brackets as the Planck constant approaches zero. In this limit where \(\hbar \to 0\), the wave function coordinates transition from the discrete representations of Hilbert space to the continuous trajectories of classical phase space. The quantum commutator between operators, \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = i\hbar \hat{C}\) with Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\), simplifies directly to the classical Poisson bracket of Hamilton-Jacobi mechanics, ensuring that the dynamical equations of quantum states smoothly recover the deterministic motion of classical particles. This mathematical reduction confirms the consistency of the quantum formalism, ensuring that the abstract geometry of Dirac notation remains grounded in the physical laws that govern the macroscopic universe.

uniformity-of-time.title: Uniformity of Time
uniformity-of-time.content:
Asserting that the fundamental laws of physics remain unchanged at every moment in history defines a key symmetry of nature. This temporal symmetry, commonly referred to as the uniformity of time, implies that the temporal origin chosen for a physical experiment is completely arbitrary, ensuring that a physical process conducted today will yield the same results as one conducted tomorrow under identical conditions. In theoretical mechanics, this uniformity is a defining characteristic of inertial reference frames, which are structured by a flat spacetime geometry with coordinate positions \(x^i\), coordinate time \(t\), and coordinate index \(\mu\). The homogeneity of time ensures that the temporal parameter flows uniformly and independently of the spatial coordinates, providing a stable background upon which the trajectories of physical systems can be mapped and analyzed. This stable temporal background is essential for the reproducibility of scientific measurements across different epochs.

The mathematical formulation of this temporal symmetry is established using Noether's theorem, which relates continuous symmetries of the Lagrangian density to physical conservation laws. For a mechanical system described by a Lagrangian function \(L(q_i, \dot{q}_i, t)\) that has no explicit dependence on coordinate time, the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to time is identically zero, written as \(\partial L / \partial t = 0\). By applying the Euler-Lagrange equations, this symmetry leads directly to the conservation of the Hamiltonian function \(H = \sum p_i \dot{q}_i - L\), which represents the total mechanical energy of the system, so that \(dH/dt = 0\). This derivation shows that the conservation of energy is not an arbitrary law, but a direct geometric consequence of the uniformity of time. This connection between symmetry and conservation represents a deep unifying principle in theoretical physics.

This uniformity allows for the definition of standard clocks, which are physical systems that oscillate with a constant frequency and provide a consistent measure of time intervals. In classical dynamics, the coordinate time parameter \(t\) is universal and absolute, flowing at the same rate for all observers regardless of their state of motion, which is formally expressed by the Galilean transformation identity \(t' = t\) in frame \(S\) and \(S'\). This absolute timeline ensures that the total dynamics of the observable universe can be mapped onto a single, coherent sequence of events, establishing a framework for scientific realism where the past and future are connected by deterministic equations of motion. The consistency of these standard clocks is a necessary assumption for the synchronization of reference frames.

In relativistic mechanics, the uniformity of time is preserved locally along the world-line of a particle by defining the proper time interval. While coordinate time becomes frame-dependent under Lorentz transformations, the proper time \(d\tau\) along a timelike trajectory remains a Lorentz invariant scalar, defined by the metric contract relation \(d\tau^2 = -g_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^\nu\) with the metric tensor \(g_{\mu\nu}\). This local uniformity ensures that physical processes, such as the decay of a particle or the vibrations of an atom, occur at a constant rate with respect to proper time in the particle's rest frame, linking physical causality directly to the local geometry of the spacetime manifold and preventing any coordinate-dependent ambiguities. This local invariance ensures that the laws of physics are locally identical for all free-falling observers.

However, in physical cosmology, the global uniformity of time is broken by the expansion history of the universe. Because the spacetime metric contains a time-dependent scale factor \(a(t)\) at time \(t\) that describes the expanding geometry of the universe, the global metric is not invariant under time translation, meaning that time-translation symmetry is lost on cosmological scales. This symmetry breaking is the physical reason why cosmological redshift causes propagating photons to lose energy, as their wavelength scales with the scale factor \(a(t)\) with photon energy \(E = h\nu\), proving that energy is not globally conserved in an expanding block universe. This cosmological result illustrates how the geometric structure of the universe shapes the conservation laws of physical fields, showing that global conservation requires a static background.

The correspondence between the relativistic proper time and the absolute time of classical mechanics is recovered in the limit where the relative velocities approach zero. In this classical limit where \(v \to 0\), the Lorentz factor \(\gamma\) contracts to unity, causing the coordinate time interval to become identical to the proper time interval, \(\Delta t \approx \Delta\tau\). The metric tensor simplifies to the flat Minkowski metric \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\), and the temporal coordinate decouples from the spatial coordinates. This continuous reduction ensures that the relativistic equations smoothly transition to the universal, uniform time of Newtonian physics, maintaining the correspondence principle across all physical scales and anchoring the theoretical models of the universe in a predictable, consistent flow. This limits the divergence between different observer coordinate systems under low-velocity conditions.
